COOPERATIVE CORPORATION — FORMATION INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Cooperative

COOPERATIVE CORPORATION PURPOSE AND MEMBERSHIP DECLARATION
The name of the corporation is Acme Cooperative. This corporation is a cooperative corporation organized under the Cooperative Corporation Law, Part 2 of Division 3 of Title 1 of the California Corporations Code (commencing with Section 12200). The purpose of this corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a corporation may be organized under the law. Acme Cooperative shall be organized and shall conduct its business primarily for the mutual benefit of its members as patrons of the corporation. providing wholesale groceries to member-owned retail stores The voting power of the members of Acme Cooperative is equal: each member entitled to vote is entitled to one vote on each matter submitted to a vote of the members. The initial street address of Acme Cooperative is 123 Main St, San Francisco, CA 94103. The name of Acme Cooperative's initial agent for service of process in California is Jordan Lee. The agent's street address in California is 123 Main St, San Francisco, CA 94103.

WHAT A COOPERATIVE CORPORATION IS AND THE PATRONAGE-BASED PURPOSE REQUIREMENT
California's Corporations Code contains a distinct statutory part governing the "cooperative corporation" — Part 2 of Division 3 of Title 1, Corp. Code §§ 12200-12704, titled the "Cooperative Corporation Law" — that is a different corporate form from an ordinary for-profit corporation formed only under the General Corporation Law, from the nonprofit public benefit, mutual benefit, and religious corporation laws, and from the for-profit benefit corporation statute, all covered elsewhere in this corpus. By its own terms, this part "is intended primarily to apply to the organization and operation of cooperatives, including, but not limited to, consumer cooperatives, worker cooperatives, and cooperatives formed for the purpose of recycling or treating hazardous waste that elect to incorporate under its provisions." The statute defining a cooperative corporation's core purpose states that a corporation formed under this part "shall be organized and shall conduct its business primarily for the mutual benefit of its members as patrons of the corporation" — that is, based on their use of the cooperative's goods, services, or marketing activities, rather than to maximize a financial return on invested capital. The same section elsewhere states that these corporations "are democratically controlled and are not organized to make a profit for themselves, as such, or for their members, as such, but primarily for their members as patrons."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "This part shall be known as the Cooperative Corporation Law. This part is intended primarily to apply to the organization and operation of cooperatives, including, but not limited to, consumer cooperatives, worker cooperatives, and cooperatives formed for the purpose of recycling or treating hazardous waste that elect to incorporate under its provisions."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 12200, California Cooperative Corporation Law, short title and stated scope (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=12200.)
  "a corporation may be formed under this part for any lawful purpose provided that it shall be organized and shall conduct its business primarily for the mutual benefit of its members as patrons of the corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 12201, California Cooperative Corporation Law, required mutual-benefit-of-members-as-patrons purpose (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=12201.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one state defines and structures this specific corporate form — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific cooperative's formation, and not a claim that every state with a cooperative corporation statute defines or structures the form identically; cooperative statutes vary by state, and some states place agricultural, consumer, worker, or housing cooperatives under separate statutes rather than one unified law. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 12200 and Cal. Corp. Code § 12201, and are treated as two independent sources. Note that this California statute's own listed scope — consumer cooperatives, worker cooperatives, and hazardous-waste or recycling cooperatives — does not on its face include agricultural cooperatives; a separate citation below (in the required-articles-content clause) reflects the statute's own cross-reference showing agricultural cooperative associations are instead organized under a distinct body of law, the Food and Agricultural Code. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation and does not determine which statute governs the formation of any specific cooperative enterprise.

ONE MEMBER, ONE VOTE: THE DEFAULT RULE AND ITS NARROW EXCEPTION
California's Cooperative Corporation Law states a one-member-one-vote rule as the governing default for member voting, in contrast to an ordinary corporation's voting power, which is generally based on the number of shares owned. The statute provides that, subject to two identified exceptions, "each member entitled to vote shall be entitled to one vote on each matter submitted to a vote of the members." This is a default that applies broadly, but it is not absolute: one of the two statutory exceptions applies specifically to a "central organization" — a cooperative whose own membership is composed, in whole or in part, of other cooperative corporations — whose articles of incorporation "may provide for unequal voting power of its members based upon the number of its members' members, the patronage of its members, or both." Even within that narrow exception, the statute preserves a voting-power floor rather than permitting it to be varied without limit: "in no event shall any member have less than one vote."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except as provided in Sections 12314 and 12484, each member entitled to vote shall be entitled to one vote on each matter submitted to a vote of the members."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 12480, California Cooperative Corporation Law, default one-member-one-vote rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=12480.)
  "The articles of incorporation of a central organization, as defined in Section 12256, organized under or subject to this part may provide for unequal voting power of its members based upon the number of its members’ members, the patronage of its members, or both. In no event shall any member have less than one vote."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 12314, California Cooperative Corporation Law, unequal voting power exception for central organizations, with a one-vote floor (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=12314.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one state structures member voting for this specific corporate form — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific cooperative's voting rules, and whether a state defaults to one-member-one-vote, and how freely that default can be varied, varies by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 12480 and Cal. Corp. Code § 12314, and are treated as two independent sources; the statute's other referenced exception, Cal. Corp. Code § 12484 (governing cumulative voting, chiefly for central organizations), was located but is not independently quoted here. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine the voting rules that apply to any specific cooperative corporation's members, and does not determine whether any specific cooperative qualifies as a "central organization" under this statute.

PATRONAGE DIVIDENDS: THE STATUTORY BASIS AND DEFINITION OF "PATRONAGE"
California's Cooperative Corporation Law ties the distribution of a cooperative's net earnings to members' patronage — their business done with the cooperative — rather than to their capital investment. The statute defining a cooperative corporation's core purpose states that "the earnings, savings, or benefits of the corporation shall be used for the general welfare of the members or shall be proportionately and equitably distributed to some or all of its members or its patrons, based upon their patronage of the corporation, in the form of cash, property, evidences of indebtedness, capital credits, memberships, or services." A separate section of the same part supplies the statutory measure of "patronage" itself: for a cooperative organized to provide goods or services, "'[p]atronage' of a patron is measured by the volume or value, or both, of a patron's purchases of products from, and use of services furnished by, the corporation, and by products and services provided by the patron to the corporation for marketing" — with a separate, work-based measure supplied elsewhere in the same section for worker cooperatives.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The earnings, savings, or benefits of the corporation shall be used for the general welfare of the members or shall be proportionately and equitably distributed to some or all of its members or its patrons, based upon their patronage (Section 12243) of the corporation, in the form of cash, property, evidences of indebtedness, capital credits, memberships, or services."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 12201, California Cooperative Corporation Law, patronage-based distribution of earnings, savings, or benefits (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=12201.)
  "“Patronage” of a patron is measured by the volume or value, or both, of a patron’s purchases of products from, and use of services furnished by, the corporation, and by products and services provided by the patron to the corporation for marketing."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 12243(a)(2), California Cooperative Corporation Law, statutory measure of "patronage" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=12243.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's own statutory basis for patronage-based distribution and its own definition of "patronage" for this specific corporate form — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific cooperative's distributions, and how a state defines and measures patronage, if at all, varies by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 12201 and Cal. Corp. Code § 12243(a)(2); the quoted sentence from § 12201 is a different sentence of that same section than the one quoted in this document's definition-and-purpose clause, and § 12243 contains a further subsection, (b), addressing the separate patronage measure for worker cooperatives, which is not independently quoted here. This document is informational only: it does not itself calculate, declare, or distribute any patronage dividend or refund for any specific cooperative, and does not address the separate question of the federal income tax treatment of patronage dividends.

LIMITS ON DISTRIBUTIONS: THE STATUTORY CAP ON RETURN PAYABLE FOR CAPITAL CONTRIBUTIONS
California's Cooperative Corporation Law caps the annual return a cooperative may pay on members' capital contributions, a limit that has no counterpart for an ordinary for-profit corporation's payments to its shareholders. The statute provides that "distributions in any fiscal year shall not exceed 15 percent, multiplied by contributions (whether by membership fees, capital credits, or otherwise) to capital." This cap applies to a specifically defined term, and that definition is itself narrower than it might first appear: a separate section defines "distribution," for purposes of this cap, to mean "the distribution of any gains, profits or dividends to any member as such, but does not include patronage distributions." Read together, the 15-percent cap constrains what a cooperative pays as a return on capital contributed by its members, while leaving patronage-based distributions — the earnings distributed based on members' business done with the cooperative, discussed elsewhere in this document — outside that specific statutory ceiling.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Distributions (Section 12235) in any fiscal year shall not exceed 15 percent, multiplied by contributions (whether by membership fees, capital credits, or otherwise) to capital."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 12451, California Cooperative Corporation Law, 15 percent annual cap on distributions measured against capital contributions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=12451.)
  "“Distribution” means the distribution of any gains, profits or dividends to any member as such, but does not include patronage distributions."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 12235, California Cooperative Corporation Law, definition of "distribution" excluding patronage distributions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=12235.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's own numeric cap on capital-return distributions for this specific corporate form — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific cooperative's distributions, and whether a state caps the return payable on capital contributions, and at what rate, varies by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 12451 and Cal. Corp. Code § 12235, and are treated as two independent sources. A related, separately enacted section, Cal. Corp. Code § 12453, also restricts a cooperative's ability to make patronage distributions out of earnings attributable to business with nonmembers, and to redeem memberships, when the cooperative is or would become unable to meet its liabilities as they mature — that solvency-linked restriction was located but is not independently quoted or relied upon in this clause. This document could not verify, and accordingly does not state, any separate statutory cap on the volume or proportion of business a California cooperative corporation may transact with nonmembers as such; no such numeric limit was found in the sections of this statute reviewed, and that sub-topic is omitted here rather than guessed at. This document is informational only: it does not itself calculate or authorize any specific distribution for any specific cooperative.

REQUIRED CONTENT OF COOPERATIVE CORPORATION ARTICLES OF INCORPORATION
California's Cooperative Corporation Law adds required content to a cooperative's articles of incorporation on top of what an ordinary corporation's articles must contain, including a mandatory statement identifying the entity as a cooperative and disclosing how member voting power and proprietary interests are structured. The statute lists what the articles "shall set forth," including the corporation's name and required agent and address information, and further requires "the following statement: 'This corporation is a cooperative corporation organized under the Cooperative Corporation Law. The purpose of this corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a corporation may be organized under the law.'" The same list requires the articles to disclose "[w]hether the voting power or the proprietary interests of the members are equal or unequal," and, if unequal, to state the general rule for determining them or that the rule will be set in the bylaws. Separately, the statute governs use of the word "cooperative" itself in a corporate name: "the names of all corporations formed under this part shall include 'cooperative,'" and no corporation may adopt that word as part of its name unless incorporated under this part or under one of several other specifically listed cooperative-type statutes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The articles of incorporation of a corporation formed under this part shall set forth: (a) The name of the corporation. (b) The following statement: “This corporation is a cooperative corporation organized under the Cooperative Corporation Law. The purpose of this corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a corporation may be organized under the law.”"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 12310, California Cooperative Corporation Law, required articles of incorporation content, including the required cooperative-status statement and voting/proprietary-interest disclosure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=12310.)
  "The names of all corporations formed under this part shall include “cooperative.” No corporation shall be formed under this part unless there is affixed or prefixed to its name some word or abbreviation which will indicate that it is a corporation, as distinguished from a natural person, a firm, or an unincorporated association."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 12311(a), California Cooperative Corporation Law, requirement that a cooperative's name include the word "cooperative" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=12311.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's own required formation-document content for this specific corporate form — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific cooperative's formation, and required articles content for a cooperative corporation varies by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 12310 and Cal. Corp. Code § 12311(a), and are treated as two independent sources; § 12310 contains further subsections, including an optional worker-cooperative election under subdivision (g), that are not independently quoted here. Notably, the naming statute's own text (§ 12311(b)) cross-references a separate body of law for a different, related cooperative form: it excepts from its restriction a corporation "incorporated as a nonprofit cooperative association under Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 54001) of Division 20 of the Food and Agricultural Code" — confirming that California's agricultural cooperatives are organized under the Food and Agricultural Code rather than under the Corporations Code Cooperative Corporation Law covered in this document; this document does not address that separate agricultural-cooperative statute. This document is informational only: it does not itself draft, file, or submit articles of incorporation for any specific cooperative, and does not itself elect any optional statutory provision, such as worker-cooperative status, on behalf of any corporation.
